mainTopic: Not permitting local stringencies in front of people (דברים המותרין ואחרים נהגו בהן איסור): rice-dough חלה, the stories of רבן גמליאל's sons, and רבה בר בר חנה's travel between ארץ ישראל and בבל
overview: This amud finishes the debate about בני חוזאי, who separated חלה from rice dough even though rice is exempt. אביי objects that one may not publicly permit something people treat as forbidden. רב יוסף answers that רב חסדא limited this rule to כותאי, but the גמרא replies that the unlearned people of חוזאי will also stretch the leniency. רב אשי then says it depends on whether the local people mostly eat rice or mostly eat grain. Returning to the rule itself, the גמרא challenges רב חסדא with a ברייתא of three stories: bathing in כבול, wide shoes in בירי, and stools in עכו. In each, the sons of רבן גמליאל respected a local stringency. The גמרא answers that towns without חכמים are treated like כותאי, and it explains the reason behind each custom. Next comes the story of רבה בר בר חנה, who hid permitted fat from scholars in בבל. אביי criticizes this as treating them like כותאי. The גמרא then explains why he could eat it there, giving two answers from אביי and רב אשי. It closes by beginning to quote another statement of his that seems to contradict his advice to his son, a point that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of אביי's objection: you may not permit it in front of them
steps.stepSummary: This amud opens with the last words of אביי's challenge to רב יוסף. You may not permit a practice in front of people who treat it as forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: You are not allowed to permit them [these practices] in their presence.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes אביי's objection to רב יוסף, who had allowed a זר to eat rice-dough 'חלה' in front of בני חוזאי. אביי says the rule forbids publicly permitting something people treat as forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בני חוזאי treated rice dough as needing חלה, even though it is really exempt. אביי argues that having a זר eat their 'חלה' in front of them publicly breaks their stringency. The rule of דברים המותרין says you may not do that.
steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts in the middle of a sentence. The first half of the rule ('דברים המותרין ואחרים נהגו בהן איסור') was said on the previous amud, and it is quoted in full later in step 6.

phrases.english: you are not allowed to permit them in their presence.
phrases.notes: This is the end of the rule that אביי quotes to challenge רב יוסף.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues אביי's challenge, which began on the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's ruling that a זר may eat rice-dough חלה in front of בני חוזאי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A known rule forbids publicly permitting something a community treats as forbidden, and רב יוסף's ruling does exactly that.

steps.title: רב יוסף answers: that rule was said only about כותאי
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף replies that רב חסדא already limited this rule to כותאי. So it does not apply to בני חוזאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But wasn't it stated about this rule that רב חסדא said: [it refers] to כותאי?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף defends his ruling. He points out that רב חסדא said the rule of 'don't permit it in front of them' applies only to כותאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף does not deny the rule. He narrows its scope: it is a special safeguard for כותאי, not for ordinary Jews. If that is right, his ruling for בני חוזאי stands.

keyTerms.meaning: but wasn't it said about it…? (introduces a known teaching)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: וְלָאו מִי אִיתְּמַר עֲלַהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: But wasn't it stated about it,
Rav Chisda said: [it refers] to Samaritans!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge by limiting the rule's scope.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the cited rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule applies to everyone, including בני חוזאי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule applies only to כותאי, so רב יוסף's ruling is fine.

steps.title: Rejection: the people of חוזאי will also stretch the leniency
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the rule applies to כותאי: they stretch leniencies too far. The people of חוזאי will do the same, so the answer fails.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason for כותאי? Because they extend the matter [to other leniencies]. These people too will extend the matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects רב יוסף's answer. It looks at the reason behind רב חסדא's limitation and shows that the same reason applies to בני חוזאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule targets כותאי because, once they hear one leniency, they wrongly apply it to other cases. בני חוזאי are unlearned, so they will also stretch it. The reason behind the rule covers them as well, and רב יוסף's defense collapses.

keyTerms.meaning: they extend / stretch the matter (to other cases)

phrases.english: Samaritans, what is the reason?
Because they extend the matter;
these people also extend the matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The attempt to exempt בני חוזאי by limiting the rule to כותאי
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The reason for the כותאי limitation (stretching leniencies) applies equally to the people of חוזאי.

steps.title: רב אשי: where most people eat rice, a זר should not eat it
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a new approach that depends on local diet. Where most people eat rice, a זר should not eat the rice 'חלה' in front of them, or they will forget the laws of חלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: We look. If most of them eat rice, a זר should not eat it in front of them, lest the law of חלה be forgotten by them.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the earlier answer failed, רב אשי offers a new way to decide. This step gives the first case, a place where most people eat rice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If rice is their main food and they see its 'חלה' eaten by a זר, they may stop separating חלה altogether. The whole idea of חלה could then be forgotten. So in such a place, their custom of separating from rice is left alone.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
We see: if most of them eat rice,
a non-priest should not eat it in front of them,
lest the law of challah be forgotten by them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב יוסף's defense was rejected, רב אשי offers a new resolution.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case by local circumstance
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There is one fixed answer for everyone about eating rice-dough חלה in public.
steps.terutzMaskana: It depends on the local staple food. In rice-eating places, a זר does not eat it.

steps.title: רב אשי: where most people eat grain, a זר should eat it
steps.stepSummary: Where most people eat grain, a זר should eat the rice 'חלה' in front of them. Otherwise they may separate חלה from one kind of dough on behalf of the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if most of them eat grain, a זר should eat it in front of them, lest they come to separate from the obligated on behalf of the exempt, and from the exempt on behalf of the obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of רב אשי's answer. In a grain-eating place, the 'חלה' from rice should be eaten by a זר in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If people think rice needs חלה, they might separate חלה from rice dough to cover wheat dough, or from wheat dough to cover rice dough. Separating across exempt and obligated dough does not work, so obligated dough would be left without valid חלה. Showing in public that rice 'חלה' is not real חלה prevents this mix-up, and here there is no risk of forgetting חלה, since they mostly eat grain anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: to separate (a gift such as חלה)

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי's rule: in rice-eating places, a זר does not eat rice 'חלה' publicly (so חלה is not forgotten). In grain-eating places, a זר does eat it publicly (so people don't separate from exempt dough on behalf of obligated dough, or the reverse).

phrases.english: And if most of them eat grain,
let a non-priest eat it in front of them,
lest they come to separate
from the obligated on behalf of the exempt,
and from the exempt on behalf of the obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב אשי's two-part answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case by local circumstance
steps.terutzMaskana: In grain-eating places, a זר eats the rice 'חלה' publicly to prevent mixing exempt and obligated dough.

steps.title: Back to the rule itself: רב חסדא limits it to כותאי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the rule of דברים המותרין to examine it directly. רב חסדא says it is speaking about כותאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter itself: Things that are permitted, but others were accustomed to treat as forbidden, you may not permit them in their presence. רב חסדא said: We are dealing with כותאי.
steps.whatsHappening: With 'גופא' the גמרא goes back to study the rule quoted earlier, on its own terms. It restates the rule and רב חסדא's limitation, setting up a challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the rule came up only as part of the חלה discussion. Now the גמרא examines whether רב חסדא is right that the rule is only for כותאי. This sets the stage for the next step, which questions that limitation.

keyTerms.meaning: 'the matter itself': returning to analyze a teaching quoted earlier
they were accustomed to treat them as forbidden

phrases.english: The matter itself: Things that are permitted
but others were accustomed to treat them as forbidden,
you are not allowed to permit them in their presence.
Rav Chisda said: We are dealing with Samaritans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the rule cited in steps 1 and 2 to examine it on its own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not permit in public what people treat as forbidden. According to רב חסדא, this applies to כותאי.

steps.title: Challenge from the brothers bathing together in כבול
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the rule really excludes ordinary Jews. A ברייתא tells how הלל, son of רבן גמליאל, respected a local stringency in כבול and did not tell the people it was permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for everyone, not? But it was taught: Two brothers may bathe together, but in כבול two brothers do not bathe together. An incident: יהודה and הלל, sons of רבן גמליאל, bathed together in כבול, and the whole city criticized them, saying: In all our days we have not seen this. הלל slipped away to the outer room and did not want to tell them: You are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא. Here are ordinary Jews, not כותאי, and a great scholar still refused to tell them their stringency was unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bathing together is permitted for brothers, but the people of כבול were strict about it. הלל gave in to their custom and stayed silent instead of permitting it. This suggests the rule of not permitting in front of them applies to everyone, not only כותאי.

keyTerms.meaning: Kabul, a town in the Galil

phrases.english: And for everyone, not?
But it was taught: Two brothers may bathe together,
but two brothers do not bathe together in Kabul.
And there was an incident with Yehuda and Hillel,
the sons of Rabban Gamliel,
who both bathed together in Kabul,
and the whole city criticized them;
they said: In all our days we have not seen this.
And Hillel slipped away and went out to the outer room,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא רָצָה לוֹמַר לָהֶן: מוּתָּרִין אַתֶּם.
phrases.english: and did not want to tell them: You are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב חסדא's limitation from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's claim that the rule applies only to כותאי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ordinary Jews in כבול kept a needless stringency, and הלל would not tell them it was permitted. So the rule seems to apply to everyone.

steps.title: Second story: wide shoes on שבת in בירי
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with a second case. The brothers wore wide shoes on שבת in בירי, the city objected, and they handed the shoes to their servants without saying 'you are permitted.'
steps.simpleTranslation: One may go out on שבת with wide shoes, but in בירי one does not go out with wide shoes on שבת. An incident: יהודה and הלל, sons of רבן גמליאל, went out with wide shoes on שבת in בירי, and the city criticized them, saying: In all our days we have not seen this. They removed them, gave them to their servants, and did not want to tell them: You are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second example from the same ברייתא, strengthening the challenge against רב חסדא. Again the brothers respected a local stringency of ordinary Jews and stayed silent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Going out on שבת with these wide shoes is permitted, but the people of בירי were strict. The brothers took the shoes off and gave them to their servants rather than correct the townspeople. This is a second case of honoring an ordinary community's stringency, which adds weight to the question on רב חסדא.
steps.whatToRemember: Stories from the ברייתא (bathing in כבול, wide shoes in בירי) show the sons of רבן גמליאל respecting ordinary Jews' needless stringencies. This challenges רב חסדא's claim that the rule is only for כותאי. A third story follows in step 9, and the answer comes in step 10.

phrases.english: One may go out with wide shoes on Shabbat,
but one does not go out with wide shoes on Shabbat in Beirei.
And there was an incident with Yehuda and Hillel,
the sons of Rabban Gamliel,
who went out with wide shoes on Shabbat in Beirei,
and the city criticized them,
and they said: In all our days we have not seen this.
And they removed them and gave them to their servants,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא רָצוּ לוֹמַר לָהֶן: מוּתָּרִין אַתֶּם.
phrases.english: and did not want to tell them: You are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a second example supporting the challenge.
steps.raayaObject: That the rule against permitting in public applies even to ordinary Jews
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא: the sons of רבן גמליאל and the wide shoes in בירי

steps.title: Third case: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the stools in עכו
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a third story. In עכו, people did not sit on gentile stools on שבת. When רבן שמעון בן גמליאל sat on them, the city objected, and he moved to the ground without saying 'you are permitted.'
steps.simpleTranslation: One may sit on gentiles' stools on שבת, but in עכו people do not sit on them. Once רבן שמעון בן גמליאל sat on such stools in עכו on שבת. The whole city criticized him and said, 'We have never seen such a thing in our lives!' He slid down onto the ground and did not want to tell them, 'You are allowed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with a third example of the same pattern. A great חכם respects a local stringency about something permitted, and he does not correct the people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case gives even more force to the קשיא from step 7. These were Jews, not כותאי, and still the חכם would not tell them the act was permitted. Three stories now point the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Gentiles' stools or benches, often used to display goods for sale

phrases.english: And one may sit on gentiles' stools on Shabbat,
but they do not sit on gentiles' stools
on Shabbat in Akko.
And there was an incident with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
who sat on gentiles' stools
on Shabbat in Akko,
and the whole city criticized him;
they said: In all our days we have never seen this.
He slid down onto the ground,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא רָצָה לוֹמַר לָהֶן: מוּתָּרִין אַתֶּם.
phrases.english: and did not want to tell them: You are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third and final case in the same ברייתא, adding weight to the challenge
steps.raayaObject: That a חכם does not permit a local stringency even to ordinary Jews
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about רבן שמעון בן גמליאל in עכו

steps.title: Distant towns are treated like כותאי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge. People in distant coastal towns rarely have חכמים among them, so they are treated like כותאי, and רב חסדא's rule applies to them too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The people of the coastal towns also have the status of כותים, because Torah scholars are not usually found among them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב חסדא. The communities in the stories were Jews, but they had the same weakness as כותאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger with כותאי is that if you permit one thing, they will stretch it to permit other things. The same danger exists in places where no חכמים live to guide people. So the rule of not telling people 'it is permitted' covers these towns as well.

keyTerms.meaning: People of the coastal or overseas towns, far from the centers of Torah
Sages are not commonly found there
They are like כותים, the Samaritans

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רב חסדא's rule is about how well-taught a community is, not only about who the people are.

phrases.english: The people of the coastal towns too,
since Sages are not commonly found among them,
are like Kutim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge built in steps 7 to 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Widening the category: these communities count as כותאי
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ordinary Jews were involved, so רב חסדא's limit to כותאי seemed wrong
steps.terutzMaskana: Towns without חכמים are treated like כותאי, so the rule stands

steps.title: The reasons for the stools and shoes are clear, but why not bathing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the stools and the wide shoes were treated as forbidden. It then asks what the reason could be for brothers not bathing together.
steps.simpleTranslation: We understand the gentiles' stools: sitting on them looks like buying and selling. We understand the wide shoes too: they might slip off, and the person would then carry them four אמות in a רשות הרבים. But bathing, why should it not be allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks for the reasons behind the three customs. Two are easy to explain, and it asks about the third, bathing. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each custom should have some real concern behind it. The stools look like business on שבת. The shoes could lead to carrying, which is an איסור דאורייתא. But two brothers bathing together seems to involve no concern at all.

phrases.english: It is understandable regarding gentiles' stools,
because it looks like buying and selling.
Wide shoes as well,
lest they slip off
and he come to carry them four cubits
in the public domain.
But bathing: what is the reason it is not allowed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the main rule to explaining the reasons for each custom
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason behind the custom that two brothers do not bathe together

steps.title: A ברייתא: people one may not bathe with
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. A man may bathe with anyone except his father, his father-in-law, his mother's husband, and his sister's husband. רבי יהודה permits bathing with one's father, and with one's mother's husband, for the sake of honoring him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: a person may bathe with anyone except his father, his father-in-law, his mother's husband, and his sister's husband. רבי יהודה allows a son to bathe with his father, because the son honors his father by helping him. The same is true for his mother's husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer by quoting a ברייתא. It lists relatives a man should not bathe with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of these men is close to a woman who is close to the bather. Seeing him unclothed could lead to improper thoughts about that relationship. רבי יהודה makes an exception where helping the man is a form of כבוד אב.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As was taught in a baraita:
A person may bathe with anyone,
except his father and his father-in-law
and his mother's husband and his sister's husband.
And Rabbi Yehuda permits it with his father
because of his father's honor,
and the same applies to his mother's husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question about bathing
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A ברייתא forbids bathing with certain relatives, including one's sister's husband

steps.title: Kabul extended the rule to two brothers
steps.stepSummary: The people of כבול added their own decree. They forbade two brothers from bathing together because it resembles bathing with a sister's husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: The people of כבול came and made a decree that two brothers should not bathe together, because of the rule about a sister's husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer. The custom in כבול was an extra fence built on top of the ברייתא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא did not forbid bathing with a brother. כבול added that stringency on its own, because brothers are similar to a sister's husband. This is why it counts as a local stringency on something permitted, which is exactly the subject of רב חסדא's rule.
steps.whatToRemember: Each of the three customs grew out of a real concern: looking like business, carrying on שבת, or improper thoughts. The חכמים respected these customs and did not undo them in front of uninformed communities.
steps.confusionAlert: The ban on brothers bathing together is not from the ברייתא. It is כבול's own addition, which is why it counts as a local stringency.

phrases.english: And they came and decreed regarding two brothers
because of a sister's husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer by linking the ברייתא to כבול's custom
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: כבול's custom about brothers is a local fence modeled on the ban on bathing with a sister's husband

steps.title: A student bathing with his teacher
steps.stepSummary: A related teaching: a תלמיד should not bathe with his רבי, but if the רבי needs his help, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: a student should not bathe with his teacher. But if the teacher needs his help, it is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more related teaching about bathing, this time about respect for one's רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the concern is different. Seeing one's רבי unclothed is disrespectful. When the רבי needs help, serving him is itself respect, much like רבי יהודה's reasoning about one's father.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא: תַּלְמִיד לֹא יִרְחַץ עִם רַבּוֹ,
phrases.english: It was taught: A student may not bathe with his teacher,
but if his teacher needs him, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: תַּלְמִיד לֹא יִרְחַץ עִם רַבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side teaching that adds to the laws of bathing
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד does not bathe with his רבי unless the רבי needs his help

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה eats the fat and hides it
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה ate fat that was permitted in ארץ ישראל but forbidden in בבל. He hid it from two visiting רבנן, and אביי said he had treated them like כותאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבה בר בר חנה came to בבל, he ate the fat over the straight part of the stomach. רב עוירא the Elder and רבה son of רב הונא came in to see him. When he saw them, he covered the food. They went and told אביי. אביי said to them: He treated you like כותאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a visitor from ארץ ישראל who ate something the people of בבל treat as forbidden. He hid it from local scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He hid the food instead of telling them it was permitted, as if the rule of not permitting in front of people applied to them. אביי's remark is a criticism: that rule is meant for כותאי and people like them, who stretch leniencies. With תלמידי חכמים he could simply have explained that it is permitted, so hiding it treated them like כותאי.

keyTerms.meaning: The fat over the straight, string-shaped part of the stomach
He covered it, he hid it
He made you, he treated you as
כותים, people who are not told about leniencies because they may misuse them

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not calling the רבנן actual כותאי. He is saying that by hiding the food, רבה בר בר חנה acted toward them the way one acts toward כותאי.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה,
phrases.english: When Rabbah bar bar Chana came (from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel),
he ate the fat over the straight part of the stomach.
Rav Avira the Elder came in to him
together with Rabbah, son of Rav Huna.
As soon as he saw them, he hid it from them.
They came and told Abaye.
He said to them: He treated you like Kutim.
phrases.notes: He hid the leniency instead of explaining it, the way one does with כותאי.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a new story that applies the earlier idea of treating people like כותאי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה בר בר חנה hid his eating of דאייתרא from local scholars instead of telling them it was permitted. אביי criticizes this: by hiding it he treated them like כותאי, even though, according to רב חסדא, only כותאי are kept from hearing a leniency.

steps.title: Doesn't the traveler have to keep both places' stringencies?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה בר בר חנה from the משנה, which says a traveler keeps the stringencies of the place he left and the place he went to.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבה בר בר חנה not hold of what we learned in the משנה: we place on him the stringencies of the place he left and the stringencies of the place he went to?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רבה בר בר חנה could eat the fat at all. Our משנה seems to say he must keep בבל's stricter custom while he is there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the rule of חומרי המקום, a traveler takes on the strict customs of both places. בבל is strict about this fat, so he should not have eaten it in בבל. Hiding the food does not solve the problem, because the act of eating itself seems forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה לֵית לֵיהּ
phrases.english: And does Rabbah bar bar Chana not hold of
that which we learned in the Mishnah:

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתְנִין עָלָיו חוּמְרֵי הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁיָּצָא מִשָּׁם
phrases.english: we place on him the stringencies of the place he left
and the stringencies of the place he went to?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה לֵית לֵיהּ הָא דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It attacks the behavior described in the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה eating דאייתרא in בבל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says a traveler must keep the strict customs of the place he goes to. בבל is strict about this fat, so he should have refrained.

steps.title: אביי: the rule does not apply when going from ארץ ישראל to בבל
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the משנה's rule applies within one region, or from בבל to ארץ ישראל. It does not apply from ארץ ישראל to בבל, because בבל follows ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: This applies from בבל to בבל, and from ארץ ישראל to ארץ ישראל, or else from בבל to ארץ ישראל. But from ארץ ישראל to בבל, it does not apply. Since we are subordinate to them, we act like them.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by limiting the משנה. He says it does not cover someone traveling from ארץ ישראל to בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people of בבל accept the authority of the חכמים of ארץ ישראל. So a person from ארץ ישראל does not need to follow בבל's stricter custom. The rule of keeping local stringencies works in only one direction between these two lands.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply only to, this rule is limited to
We are subordinate to them, we defer to them

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הָנֵי מִילֵּי מִבָּבֶל לְבָבֶל,
phrases.english: Abaye said: This applies only from Bavel to Bavel,
and from Eretz Yisrael to Eretz Yisrael,
or also from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael.
But from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel, no.
Since we (in Bavel) are subordinate to them,
we act in accordance with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הָנֵי מִילֵּי מִבָּבֶל לְבָבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the challenge by limiting the scope of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה applies to every journey, so the traveler must keep בבל's stringency.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה does not apply to travel from ארץ ישראל to בבל, because בבל follows ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: רב אשי: he planned to return home
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives another answer. Even going from ארץ ישראל to בבל, the rule applies only to someone who is not planning to return. רבה בר בר חנה was planning to return.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: You can even say the rule applies from ארץ ישראל to בבל. But it applies only when he does not plan to return, and רבה בר בר חנה planned to return.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a different answer to the same challenge. The key factor is whether the traveler intends to go back home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי accepts that the משנה can apply even from ארץ ישראל to בבל. He limits it in another way: only someone who settles permanently takes on local stringencies. A visitor who plans to go home keeps his own place's custom.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers for why a traveler from ארץ ישראל may follow his home custom in בבל. אביי says בבל follows ארץ ישראל. רב אשי says he intends to return home.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מֵאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבָבֶל,
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: You can even say the rule applies from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel;

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּאֵין דַּעְתּוֹ לַחֲזוֹר,
phrases.english: but that is only where he does not intend to return,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה דַּעְתּוֹ לַחֲזוֹר הֲוָה.
phrases.english: and Rabbah bar bar Chana intended to return.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מֵאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבָבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It gives a second, different answer to the same challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making a distinction based on the traveler's intent
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anyone who travels must keep the new place's stringencies.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only someone who does not plan to return takes on the new place's stringencies.

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה tells his son not to eat it
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה tells his son never to eat this fat, whether or not his father is present. He himself saw רבי יוחנן eat it, but his son did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said to his son: My son, do not eat it, not in front of me and not when I am away. I saw רבי יוחנן eat it, and רבי יוחנן is worthy to be relied on, in his presence and when he is not present. You did not see him, so do not eat it, whether in front of me or not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה instructs his son, who lives in בבל, to follow the strict custom. The son may not rely on his father's report alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father relies on what he saw רבי יוחנן do. Since the son never saw it himself, he should not rely on it, even when his father is with him. This sets up the next step, which will compare this view with another statement of רבה בר בר חנה.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה לִבְנֵיהּ:
phrases.english: Rabbah bar bar Chana said to his son:
My son, do not eat it,
neither in my presence nor when I am not present.

phrases.aramaic: אֲנִי שֶׁרָאִיתִי אֶת רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁאָכַל —
phrases.english: I, who saw Rabbi Yochanan eat it:

phrases.aramaic: כְּדַי הוּא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לִסְמוֹךְ עָלָיו
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan is worthy to be relied upon
both in his presence and not in his presence.
You did not see him,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא תֹּאכַל בֵּין בְּפָנַי בֵּין שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנַי.
phrases.english: so do not eat it, whether in my presence or not in my presence.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה לִבְנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It continues the story of רבה בר בר חנה and the fat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who personally saw a great חכם act leniently may rely on him. Someone who did not see it, and lives in a strict place, may not eat it, even with the witness standing next to him.

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this statement of רבה בר בר חנה conflicts with another of his statements. It begins quoting a story he heard from רבי יוחנן בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And his statement disagrees with his other statement. For רבה בר בר חנה said: רבי יוחנן בן אלעזר told me: Once I followed רבי שמעון בן רבי יוסי בן לקוניא into the garden...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It announces a contradiction between two statements of רבה בר בר חנה and begins quoting the second one, which continues in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far, רבה בר בר חנה said one may rely on a חכם only if one saw him act personally. The גמרא now brings a story he told in someone else's name. It will suggest a different approach to the question of when a person may rely on someone else's leniency.

keyTerms.meaning: His own statement disagrees with his own other statement

steps.confusionAlert: The story is not finished here. Wait for the next section to see exactly what the contradiction is.

phrases.english: And his statement disagrees with his own other statement.
For Rabbah bar bar Chana said:

phrases.aramaic: סָח לִי רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar told me:
Once I entered,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן לָקוֹנְיָא לַגִּינָּה,
phrases.english: following Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya, into the garden,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It sets up a contradiction against what רבה בר בר חנה told his son.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר בר חנה's instruction to his son
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another report from רבה בר בר חנה seems to take a different view on relying on a leniency. The details continue on the next amud.
